FLASHCARD SET · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Music Room flashcards.

Fifty-three cards from the school’s Music Room: every instrument on the shelf, the words music uses — beat, melody, tempo, volume — and the people who fill the room with sound. Every card carries its picture word, a sound to make together and one tiny game — the whole room, ready to print.

These cards belong to Class 23 · Music Room on the Kiddo School learning path.

HOW TO USE THESE CARDS

Four ways that work.

You do not need a plan or a printer schedule. Pick one idea, try it for two minutes and see what happens.

  1. 01

    March to the beat

    Tap a steady beat on a pot, a box or your knees and march around the room exactly on it. Slow the beat down, speed it up — the tempo card is the boss and legs love a rule they can hear.

  2. 02

    Play loud and quiet

    Sing one song two ways: as loud as the volume card allows, then as quietly as a whisper. Loud and quiet is the first music contrast children own — and it tidies a noisy room better than any request.

  3. 03

    Hunt the instruments

    Play one favourite song and hunt for the instruments you can hear — a drum, a piano, a bell. Then find those cards in the set and lay them on the floor in the order you heard them.

  4. 04

    Start a kitchen band

    Pot-lid cymbals, rice-in-a-jar maracas, a shoebox guitar: match your homemade band to the real cards and play one song together. The people cards — band, duet, solo — decide who plays when.

      Accordion Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A red accordion with rainbow bellows — the instrument that sings by breathing. Squeeze it shut and the air rushes out through reeds, which makes this the noisiest hug in the whole Music Room.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      An accordion makes music with air. Two wooden boxes hold reeds — thin tongues of metal that quiver when air rushes past — and the bellows between them pump that air in and out.

      What does it sound like?

      It wheezes, swells and sings all at once — a full oom-pah sound from one instrument. Push the bellows fast for a lively tune, slow them down for a long, breathy note.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      The accordion gives movement a sound. Its push-pull rhythm matches the push-pull of walking, clapping and rocking, so children feel rhythm in their arms before they can name it.

      Say it together

      “Squeeze it out, push it in — eee-ahh, eee-ahh! The accordion sings when it breathes, just like you do.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Stand up, hold an imaginary accordion and pump your arms while you hum one long note — big arms out, small arms in. Pump faster and hear your hum speed up, just like real bellows.

      Quick parent note

      The accordion is the star of polka and French café songs. If you play one of those during the week, your child will spot the sound straight away — “the squeeze one!”

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Accordion lesson on the Learning Path.

      Bagpipes Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Bagpipes — a bag full of air, pipes sticking out and a sound that carries across a whole valley. This card starts wonderful arguments about whether it is singing or complaining. It is both.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      Bagpipes are a bag, a mouthpipe to fill it, and finger-holes on a melody pipe. The player keeps the bag full by blowing and squeezes the air out through the pipes with one arm.

      What does it sound like?

      A loud, steady drone under a skirling tune. The drone never stops — which is why bagpipes are played outdoors, at parades and at parties with thick walls.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      One sound that never stops is a brand-new idea for small ears. The bagpipe drone lets children hear the difference between a sound that holds and sounds that hop.

      Say it together

      “Fill the bag with air and squeeze — a long, loud, droning nyeee-ahhh that never stops for breath.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Blow up a paper bag, hold it shut and squeeze slowly while you hum — a two-second bagpipe. Then squeeze faster for a silly, stuttering version and let the giggles tune themselves.

      Quick parent note

      Scotland is famous for bagpipes, but many countries play their own version. If a parade passes nearby this month, drop everything and listen — that is the card, live.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Bagpipes lesson on the Learning Path.

      Banjo Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A banjo — round body, long neck, and a twang you can hear across a garden. Its skin face makes every plink brighter than a guitar, and its plucking rhythm is made for dancing feet.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A banjo is a drum with a neck: a round skin or plastic face stretched over a body, a long neck with frets, and strings you pluck with your fingers or a pick.

      What does it sound like?

      A fast, twinkly twang that sits on top of a song. Banjo players roll their fingers across the strings so the sound never stops moving — that rolling is the banjo’s signature.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      The banjo’s rolling sound teaches speed. Children hear fast notes made calmly and learn that quick music can still be relaxed — useful news for every hurried toddler.

      Say it together

      “Pling-pling-pling! The banjo twangs like a rubber band on a biscuit tin — bright, bouncy and quick.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Stretch a rubber band over an empty tub and pluck it short and long — a one-string banjo. Pluck near the edge for a high pling, near the middle for a low one, and count your strings of tins.

      Quick parent note

      The banjo grew up in America’s folk and bluegrass music. Two banjos never sound quite alike — if you find one in a song this week, ask: “faster or slower than ours?”

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Banjo lesson on the Learning Path.

      Bass Drum Flashcard for Preschoolers

      The biggest drum in the room — the bass drum. You do not hear it so much as feel it in your chest: one big BOOM that holds the whole band together like a heartbeat in boots.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A bass drum is a very large drum stood on its side, struck with a big soft mallet. In a band or orchestra it stands at the back and marks the strongest beats.

      What does it sound like?

      It goes BOOM on the important beats and stays quiet in between. Marching bands walk to it; orchestras use it for thunder, cannon shots and other wonderful crashes.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Feeling a boom in the chest is rhythm made physical. Children who pat the beat while a big drum sounds are learning to keep steady time — the first skill every drummer needs.

      Say it together

      “BOOM… BOOM… BOOM. Slow and huge — the bass drum is the floor of the music.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Pat the floor on every BOOM while a march plays — pat, step, pat, step. Then swap: stamp on the boom, pat on the quiet. Your living room is now a parade.

      Quick parent note

      Every drum family has its giant. Next time your child bangs a pot, ask: “is that a little drum or the big bass boom?” The answer shapes how hard they hit.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Bass Drum lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Bells Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A row of bells — the plinkiest instrument in the room. Each bell holds one note, so playing a tune is a walk along a rainbow: one bell, one colour, one clean little plink each step.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A set of bells is many small tuned bells in a row, played one by one with fingers or little mallets. Big versions hang in towers; toy versions sit on a table and wait for small hands.

      What does it sound like?

      Bright, round, silvery plinks. Struck once, a bell rings on and on by itself, getting quieter and quieter — a long tale from one tiny tap.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Bells connect seeing and hearing: one visible bell, one single note. Children who tap a bell row discover that notes come in steps — the doorway to every melody they will ever learn.

      Say it together

      “Plink… plink… plink! Little bells say one clean note each — ding goes every single one.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Line up three cups upside down and tap them with a spoon — one high, one middle, one low if you can. Play a three-note bell song of your own and ring it twice.

      Quick parent note

      Bells are the oldest reminder sound in the world — school bells, door bells, church bells. Point out every real bell you meet and your card set starts playing all over town.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Bells lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Castanets Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Castanets — two little shells that click together in your hand. They are pocket-sized, they are fast, and they turn any hand into the tiniest drum kit in the Music Room.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      Castanets are two hollow shells joined by a cord. Hold one shell in your palm, snap the other against it with your fingers — Spanish flamenco dancers have used them for centuries.

      What does it sound like?

      A dry, quick click-click-click, like a woodpecker with rhythm. Fast clicks sound excited; slow clicks sound like a tiny horse walking.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Clicking castanets builds a giant skill quietly: waiting. The space between clicks matters as much as the clicks — children feel rests for the first time without any words at all.

      Say it together

      “Click-click-clickity-click! Castanets talk with their mouths shut — the fastest chatter in the room.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Click a rhythm with your tongue against the roof of your mouth — click-click… click! Hands free castanets. Then click fast like a spider, slow like a snail, and ask which is which.

      Quick parent note

      No castanets at home? Two spoons or two bottle tops back-to-back click just as well. The sound is small, so this is the perfect instrument for restaurants and waiting rooms.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Castanets lesson on the Learning Path.

      Cello Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A cello — a violin’s giant cousin that sits on the floor and hums like a friendly grandfather. Its deep, warm voice is the closest thing the orchestra has to a human singing low.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A cello is a big wooden body with four strings and a bow. It stands on a spike, and the player sits behind it, drawing the bow across the strings with one hand while fingers press notes.

      What does it sound like?

      Deep, round, singing notes — the cello can purr like a lullaby or growl like thunder. It often plays the part of the song that makes everyone feel calm or sad or cosy.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Low sounds calm busy bodies. A cello card is worth its weight on difficult afternoons: children who lean into deep sounds often slow down with them, no instructions needed.

      Say it together

      “Mmmmmm — low and warm, like a big dog humming. The cello sings with a bow instead of a mouth.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Hum your lowest mmmmm and rub one hand up your other arm like a bow — long and smooth. Big slow arm, low slow hum: that is cello breathing, and it works on grown-ups too.

      Quick parent note

      Cellos must be their size, so players sit — that is why the cello leans on the floor. If your child hugs the card like a cello and strums it, the card is doing its job.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Cello lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Clarinet Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A clarinet — a long black pipe with silver keys and a voice like smooth honey. Blow past a thin wooden reed inside its mouthpiece and the pipe turns your breath into a wobbly, wonderful song.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A clarinet is a black tube with a reed — a thin sliver of cane — strapped to its mouthpiece. Blowing makes the reed buzz, the tube makes the buzz sing, and fingers open and close the keys.

      What does it sound like?

      Silky and swoopy. Clarinets can slide from a purr to a squeak in one breath, which is why they get the cat parts, the sneaky parts and the lovely sleepy parts in orchestral stories.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      The clarinet’s wobble is a friend of long exhales. Children chase its smooth sound by breathing out slowly — the same breath control that later calms tears and powers swimming.

      Say it together

      “Whooooo — wobbly and smooth, like blowing across a bottle with a straw. The clarinet giggles when it plays high.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Blow across the top of an empty bottle — wh0000! That airy hoot is a bottle clarinet. Fill it with a little water and the note climbs higher: your clarinet just grew shorter.

      Quick parent note

      A clarinet reed is thinner than a crisp and just as breakable — real players carry spares. If your child loves the squeaky-cat sound, Peter and the Wolf has a whole clarinet cat waiting.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Clarinet lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Cymbals Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Cymbals — two golden plates that crash when they meet. They are the loudest yes in the Music Room: one hit and the whole song lights up like a sparkler, then fizzes slowly away.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      Cymbals are round plates of brass. Hold one in each hand by the straps and crash them sideways together — or hang one up and strike it with a mallet, drum-kit style.

      What does it sound like?

      A bright, shimmery crash with a long tail of fizz. Cymbals mark the biggest moments: the start, the finish, the surprise. Between crashes they can hiss softly like a snake with good manners.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      The cymbal crash teaches the whole arc of a sound: big start, long fade. Children watch and hear a sound die away — an early lesson in quiet that no lecture can match.

      Say it together

      “CRASH! …sssssssss… One hit and a long, sparkly tail — cymbals are the fireworks of the band.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Crash your hands together high in the air, then let them sink slowly to the floor while your voice goes sssssss — the crash getting smaller. Big crash, tiny crash, and one crash with a yawn.

      Quick parent note

      Real cymbals are loud — the card lets you crash as often as you like. For a softer home version, two pot lids make an honest clang with none of the neighbours joining in.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Cymbals lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Drum Kit Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A drum kit — one chair, four limbs and a whole family of drums and cymbals arranged around them. The drummer plays everything at once: boom with a foot, tsh with an arm, tap-tap with the other.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A drum kit is a set — bass drum, snare, toms and cymbals — built around one seat so one player can reach everything. Feet work the bass drum and a pedal; hands take sticks and brushes.

      What does it sound like?

      The whole rhythm of a band in one place: the boom that keeps time, the backbeat that makes shoulders dance, the tsh that polishes every fourth beat.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Drumming a kit means doing two different rhythms at once — a brain party called coordination. Even patting head-rubbing-tummy versions builds the same two-hands-two-jobs wiring.

      Say it together

      “Boom-tsh, boom-boom-tsh! The drum kit is four rhythms at the same time — feet and hands, all talking together.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Sit on a chair: pat your knees for the toms, stamp one foot for the bass boom, clap for the tsh. Now put them together — boom, clap, knees-knees — and you are a kit.

      Quick parent note

      Kitchen drum kits are a proud tradition: pots for toms, lids for cymbals, a box for the boom. Decide the ending signal first — one big crash means the song is done.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Drum Kit lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Drum Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A drum — the red-and-yellow heart of the Music Room with two mallets ready. Drums were the first instruments humans ever made, and they are still the first one every child plays: hands, surface, joy.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A drum is a hollow body with a skin stretched tight over the top. Hit the skin with hands or mallets and the air inside pushes back with a boom — big drums boom low, small drums tap high.

      What does it sound like?

      The beat-keeper. Every other instrument listens to the drum for when to move. A steady drum can make a whole room walk in step without a single word.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Drumming is the straightest road to steady rhythm, and steady rhythm underpins walking, talking and later reading. Big mallet hits also finish the job of any busy afternoon.

      Say it together

      “Boom boom boom-boom-boom! The drum says what your heart says — tap it and it answers back.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Pat your knees — boom. Pat a cushion — boom. Pat the sofa arm — boooooom. Play a drum tour of the house and rate each surface: bouncy boom, flat tap or forbidden bell.

      Quick parent note

      A hand drum wants loose wrists, not fists. Show patting rather than hitting and the drum becomes a conversation: you tap two, your child answers three, and the song starts itself.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Drum lesson on the Learning Path.
