      Flute Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A flute — a slim silver pipe that sings on nothing but breath. No strings, no reed: you blow across a little hole and the air inside the tube spins into the highest, cleanest song in the orchestra.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A flute is a metal tube held sideways. The player blows across an opening near one end — not into it, across it, like blowing over a bottle top — and presses keys to change the note.

      What does it sound like?

      High, clear, gliding notes. Flutes get the bird songs, the morning songs and the bits of music that float above everyone else like a kite.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      The flute is pure breath control, the skill behind calm. Children who practise long airy whoooo sounds are literally practising slow exhales — music and self-settling in one hiss.

      Say it together

      “Whooooo-ooo! Light and airy, like blowing over a bottle’s mouth — the flute is breath turned into birdsong.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Hold an empty bottle and blow gently across its mouth until it sings — that is exactly how a flute works. Now try short hoots, a long swoop, and a bottle lullaby of three notes.

      Quick parent note

      Flutes appear in every fairy-tale soundtrack because birds get the flute. If a bird sings outside, whistle-who back at it — a two-note flute conversation is a legitimate morning activity.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Flute lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      French Horn Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A French horn — brass tubing wound into a great circle with a wide bell like a flower opening. It looks like a snail shell and sounds like a golden sunset: round, warm and far away.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A French horn is a very long brass tube coiled into loops. The player buzzes their lips into a small mouthpiece, presses valves with one hand — and tucks the other hand inside the bell to shape the sound.

      What does it sound like?

      Round, noble, glowing notes. Horns play the hunting calls, the hero entrances and the warm blanket under the whole orchestra — the sound every storybook forest has.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      The horn’s mellow call is perfect for far-away pretend play. Children answer horn calls across the room or the garden, and distance games build big breath and big listening at once.

      Say it together

      “Mwooooah — long and golden, like a voice singing through a seashell. The horn calls across mountains.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Curl your hands around your mouth like a horn bell and call mwoooah across the room. Answer each other back and forth — one call each, waiting for the echo. That is a horn conversation.

      Quick parent note

      The hand inside the bell is the secret: it makes the sound rounder or brighter. If your child “plays horn” with a rolled paper cone, the forest call is historically accurate.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the French Horn lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Gong Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A gong — a huge round bronze disc on a frame, waiting with the patience of a mountain. One mallet stroke and the whole room fills with a shimmering hum that rolls on and on and on.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A gong is a wide, flat disc of hammered bronze hung from a frame. You strike the middle with a big soft mallet — and then you wait, because a gong is never played twice in a hurry.

      What does it sound like?

      One enormous, wobbly hum that starts loud and melts slowly into shivers. Small concerts start with it; big announcements end with it. The gong is the sound of here-we-go and at-last.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      A gong’s long fade is the deepest quiet-listening exercise there is: the whole family goes still, following one sound to its end. Silence that ends a gong feels like a game, not a punishment.

      Say it together

      “GOOOOOOOONG… one hit, and the sound keeps travelling like ripples on a pond.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Strike an imaginary gong, then freeze and listen until your invisible sound completely disappears — count how long it lasts. Quiet game champion gets tomorrow’s first mallet.

      Quick parent note

      Gongs come from Asia, where families own them for announcements and ceremonies. A real gong is played exactly once per idea — the pause after the boom is half the music.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Gong lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Guitar Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A guitar — six strings, a wooden waist and a sound that fits under anyone’s arm. Strum it gently for a lullaby, strum it loudly for a party: the guitar is the most bring-alongable instrument there is.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A guitar is a wooden box with a hole under six strings. Fingers of one hand press the strings against the neck; the other hand strums or plucks, and the box makes the strings big enough to hear.

      What does it sound like?

      Warm chords and cheerful plinks. Guitars carry campfire songs, lullabies and rock’n’roll — sometimes all three in one afternoon if the player is six.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      A guitar responds to the tiniest touch, which makes it the perfect first real instrument: brush a string, get a note, brush harder, get louder. Cause and effect never sounded better.

      Say it together

      “Strum-strum-strum! The guitar hums when you brush all its strings at once — like petting a cat that sings.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Stretch rubber bands of different thicknesses over a shoebox with a hole cut in the lid — a box guitar. Pluck each band: thick string low, thin string high. Line up three and play a chord.

      Quick parent note

      Real guitars come in half sizes for small players. Until then, the shoebox version teaches every part that matters: strings, plucking, and the magical hole in the middle.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Guitar lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Harmonica Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A harmonica — ten little holes, a shirt pocket and a whole band inside. Breathe out for one note, breathe in for another: it is the only instrument that plays while you are simply breathing.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A harmonica is a small bar with metal reeds inside, one behind each hole. Blowing through a hole makes one note; drawing air back through it makes a different note — no buttons at all.

      What does it sound like?

      A wailing, happy little sound that fits folk songs, train songs and blues. It sits right beside the mouth, so players can hold a harmonica and clap, tap or dance at the same time.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      The harmonica’s blow-draw pattern teaches breath in both directions — out and in — which makes it a secret breathing exercise shaped like a toy. Small hands can hold it from age two.

      Say it together

      “Hoo-hooo — hiiin! Blow a note, breathe back a note. The harmonica turns breathing into a tune.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Hum a note out through pursed lips, then breathe the same note back in — hooo-iii. Do it four times slowly: that is a harmonica warm-up, and it doubles as settling-down magic.

      Quick parent note

      Harmonicas ride in pockets and play on street corners, campfires and front porches. If you ever find one, remember the rule of the card: out is a note, back is another note.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Harmonica lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Harp Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A harp — a tall golden frame with strings like a fountain frozen mid-sparkle. Pluck one string for a plink, sweep all of them for a glissando: the harp is the sound of magic deciding to happen.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A harp stands as tall as its player, with dozens of strings stretched across a curved frame. Players pluck the strings with their fingers — harps are older than written music itself.

      What does it sound like?

      Sparkly, liquid plinks and famous rising glissandos — the sweep of a thumb across every string in order. Harps play the dream parts: angels, moonlight, the moment before a wish.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Harp strings are a number line you can hear: shortest string highest, longest lowest. Children who pluck a harp — or a rubber-band stand-in — meet size and pitch as one idea.

      Say it together

      “Plink… plinnnng… and whoosh up all the strings — the harp does sparkles better than anybody.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Stretch several rubber bands across a baking tray — short ones and long ones. Plink each: short band high, long band low. Now sweep a thumb across them all — home glissando.

      Quick parent note

      The harp glissando is the cheapest wow in music: one finger, every note, in order. If your child sweeps the card like strings, that motion is the real technique, just ask any harpist.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Harp lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Maracas Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Maracas — a pair of shakers, one for each hand, filled with seeds or beads. Shake once for a chik, shake fast for a rrrrattle: they are the friendliest instrument in the room and the hardest to put down.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      Maracas are hollow balls on handles with something small rattling inside — dried seeds the old way, beads the toy way. They come in pairs so both hands stay busy.

      What does it sound like?

      A crisp, sandy rattle that rides on top of the beat. Shake on every tick and a song grows hips; shake only on the loud beats and a song grows boots.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Maracas make rhythm instant — no technique gate at all. Shaking also builds the wrist control that later serves spoons, whisks, paintbrushes and pencils. Sneaky, cheerful homework.

      Say it together

      “Chik-chik-chiki-chik! The maracas rattle like seeds dancing in a pod — one shake, two shake, shake-shake-shake.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Fill a bottle with a spoonful of rice, screw the lid tight and shake: chik! Two bottles, one per hand. Now shake only when the music is loud and freeze when it goes quiet.

      Quick parent note

      Maracas come from Latin America, where pairs are played call-and-answer: one player asks, the other answers. At home, that means you shake a rhythm and your child shakes it back.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Maracas lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Microphone Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A smiling microphone — not an instrument you play, but one that plays YOU. It takes the smallest voice in the room and hands it back the size of a stadium. Everyone stands straighter holding one.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A microphone listens to your voice and turns the sound into a signal, so speakers can play it back bigger. This one on the card has a happy face — microphones hear a lot of songs.

      What does it do?

      It makes voices big. In the Music Room it stands for every moment someone takes a breath, says hello-world into the mic and becomes a singer for exactly one song.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      A pretend microphone gives shy voices permission. Speaking one line into a hairbrush mic is a game; being heard is the result. Confidence has rarely had a cheaper prop.

      Say it together

      “La-la-LAAAA! Sing into your fist-microphone and let it grow your voice as big as a garden.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Hold a hairbrush or wooden spoon as your mic and announce something wonderful: “Good evening! Tonight we will eat spaghetti!” Then pass the mic — every person gets one announcement.

      Quick parent note

      The rule of real microphones: they only make you bigger, never better. Warm-ups first — then the song. A hairbrush mic also survives being dropped, which builds brave performers.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Microphone lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Stage Microphone Flashcard for Preschoolers

      The stage microphone — yellow handle, black grille, switch on the side: the mic that lives on concert stands. This is the grown-up brother of the smiling card, and it means the show is about to start.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      Stage microphones are handheld mics with a switch and a wind grille — the ball of mesh that keeps breath pops out of the sound. Singers hold them close and let the speakers do the shouting.

      What does it do?

      The show-starting sound: a finger-tap test, a count of three, then the first note, bigger than life. Stage mics also travel — singers swing them, lean on stands and take them worldwide.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Two microphone cards is a sneaky matching game: same word, different pictures. Same word for two things happens all the time in real life — and spotting it is real reading work.

      Say it together

      “One-two, one-two! Tapping the mic gently and saying one-two is how every show begins — testing, testing!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Compare the two microphone cards side by side: what is the same, what is different? Then stage a show — one mic for the singer, one for the announcer, and one-two-one-two to open.

      Quick parent note

      Real stage mics are almost always black; the yellow handle makes this one findable in a toy box. If your child announces the dinner menu tonight, the card has done a full show.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Stage Microphone lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Oboe Flashcard for Preschoolers

      An oboe — a slim black pipe with a tiny double reed and a bright, nasal, unforgettable voice. When the orchestra tunes up, everyone listens to the oboe: it gives the A that the whole room follows.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      An oboe is a black tube with a double reed — two thin reeds tied together that buzz against each other when you blow. Small reed, small tube, big personality.

      What does it sound like?

      A clear, penetrating, slightly goosey song. Oboes play the sweet sad lines and the comic farmyard ones, and before every concert they play one long A for everyone to tune to.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      The oboe is the orchestra’s tuning leader — proof that the smallest instrument can hold the biggest job. Children who feel small will take that trade personally, and rightly.

      Say it together

      “Nasally neee-nah — a bit like a happy duck with excellent manners. The oboe quacks beautifully.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Fold a strip of paper in half, hold the folded end between your thumbs and blow — a grass reed quacks like an oboe. If it honks, congratulations: you are holding a real reed principle.

      Quick parent note

      Two reeds instead of one is the oboe’s whole difference from the clarinet. Duck call or duck-adjacent honk is the correct first reaction — the oboe has heard it all before.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Oboe lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Piano Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A piano — eighty-eight keys in neat black and white, low notes on the left, high on the right. It is a harp wearing a keyboard: press a key, a little hammer taps a string, and a note steps out.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A piano has strings inside, but you never touch them. Each key is a lever for a little hammer: press down, the hammer strikes its string and lets go — that is why piano notes ring and fade.

      What does it sound like?

      Everything at once. The piano plays melody in the right hand, chords in the left, loud thunder, soft rain — one player, a whole orchestra arranged in black and white.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      The keyboard is a map children can see: left is low, right is high, every key one step. Early piano play quietly installs counting, order and left-right — the print-readiness shelf.

      Say it together

      “Plink plink plonk! Walk your fingers up the keys — the further right you go, the smaller the mouse squeaks.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Draw eight paper keys on a strip, tape it to a table and play with one finger: middle C, then a step right, then a run home. Squeeze the sponge — the louder the piano, the squishier the play.

      Quick parent note

      Pianos are percussion AND strings, which is why the card family claims it happily. If a real one is nearby, one finger tunes are legitimate: Twinkle first, chaos second, both count.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Piano lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Piccolo Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A piccolo — half the flute, twice the sparkle. It plays the very highest notes in the orchestra, the ones that thread through a whole song like a needle pulling gold. Small pipe, enormous presence.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A piccolo is a mini flute — half the length, an octave higher. Same sideways blowing, same keys, but the air column is so short the notes shoot up where only dogs and piccolos live.

      What does it sound like?

      The glitter on top. In marches the piccolo rides the melody like a flag; in orchestras it cuts through a hundred players with one bright thread.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      High and low is a first music contrast, and the piccolo is the top of the height chart. Pair its card with the tuba’s and the whole vertical world of sound snaps into place.

      Say it together

      “Fweeee! Sharp and sparkly, like a whistle that learned music. You will hear the piccolo over everyone.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Sing a note as high as you can — your piccolo voice. Now your lowest — your tuba voice. Play high-low-high-low with your hands marking up and down, and let a sibling call the shots.

      Quick parent note

      Piccolo players sit beside the flute because it is literally a small flute. If a bird sings very high and thin, blame the piccolo section — historically this is the correct joke.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Piccolo lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Recorder Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A recorder — the clean plastic pipe with a whistle mouth, waiting in a school drawer near you. Blow gently and it sings a pure, simple note: for millions of children, the recorder IS the first instrument.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A recorder is a tube with a whistle mouthpiece — the air splits on an edge and sings — plus finger holes along the front and a thumb hole behind. Fingers decide which note you get.

      What does it sound like?

      A soft, steady, honey-simple tone. Recorders play old dances, renaissance tunes and every beginner’s first Hot Cross Buns — three notes, enormous pride.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      The recorder is honest: too hard a blow squeaks, gentle breath sings. That instant feedback teaches breath control better than any lecture — and finger-hole order is counting you can hear.

      Say it together

      “Whoooo — clean and simple, like a bird whistle with a straight face. Gentle breath, pretty note.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Cover the holes with a toilet-roll tube and hum through it — a pretend recorder. Real one? Blow SOFTLY with the thumb hole covered for low notes, open for high, and brace for Hot Cross Buns.

      Quick parent note

      Every recorder squeak is information, not failure: too much air. Model a whisper-blow, then hand it over. Three honest notes played gently beat ten honked loudly every single time.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Recorder lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Saxophone Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A saxophone — golden brass all curled up with a reed in its mouth and jazz in its lungs. It bends, it swoops, it growls on purpose: the sax is the instrument that sounds like it is telling you a story.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A saxophone is brass like a trumpet but plays with a vibrating reed like a clarinet — the best of both. The player’s fingers press keys, and the breath bends each note up into the song.

      What does it sound like?

      A warm, husky, bendable voice that laughs in jazz bands and cries in slow songs. No other instrument swaggers quite so honestly.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Bending a note — swooping up into it — is the sax’s signature, and children imitate it instantly with their voices. That sliding game sharpens ears for pitch like nothing flat does.

      Say it together

      “Wah-wah-wahhhoo! Smooth and bendy, like a voice made of brass. The saxophone slides between notes on purpose.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Sing aaaa and swoop up into it from underneath — waaaa-AAA. That bend is saxophone breathing. Do three: a sleepy bend, a surprised bend and a bend that answers the question “dinner?”

      Quick parent note

      The saxophone was invented to be the loudest, softest, most voice-like instrument at once — its inventor would be pleased. Fat cat jazz with a sax in it counts as a listening lesson.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Saxophone lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Sitar Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A sitar — a long neck, a gourd body and strings that buzz on purpose. Its shimmering, swinging sound comes from India, and once your ear learns its buzz you will spot it in any song on the radio.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A sitar has a big round body, a very long neck and movable bridges. Strings run over curved bridges, and that curve makes every plucked note buzz and shimmer — the sitar’s signature.

      What does it sound like?

      A rippling, buzzing, glittering song. Sitar players slide along the neck between notes, so melodies pour like water instead of stepping like stairs.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      The sitar is a beautiful argument that different is delicious: same plucking idea as a guitar, utterly different world of sound. New sound textures grow flexible, curious listeners.

      Say it together

      “Bzzziiiing — a plink that shivers! The sitar’s strings buzz like a happy bee with a melody.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Hum one note while wiggling it up and down — oooo-WII-oooo. That wobble is what a sitar does to every note. Then sing a tiny tune entirely in wiggles and vote on the best one.

      Quick parent note

      The buzz is the feature: curved bridges let strings ring against themselves. A sitar piece for sleepy afternoons is called raga — ask for one with rain in the title and report back.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Sitar lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Tambourine Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A tambourine — a drum skin with little metal jingles set in the rim, so every slap comes with confetti. Tap it, shake it, slap it on your knee: it is three instruments that decided to travel together.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A tambourine is a small round frame with a skin across the top and pairs of tiny metal discs — jingles — fitted into slots around the rim. Hit it and both parts answer at once.

      What does it sound like?

      A slap plus a shimmer. Held high it shakes like maracas; slapped on the knee it snaps like a snare drum; rolled on the skin it hisses like a snake doing a drum solo.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      The tambourine’s two sounds — thump and jingle — teach loud and soft layers in one hold. It also demands nothing: the very first tap is already a success story.

      Say it together

      “Tap-shake-shake! The tambourine says boom with its face and jingle-jangle with its edges.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Slap the card on your knee — tap! Then shake it in the air — jangle! Play tap-tap-SHAKE, tap-tap-SHAKE, and end with the tambourine held high for one long overhead rattle. Encore rules apply.

      Quick parent note

      No tambourine? A plate with four bottle-cap pairs taped around the rim is the honest home version. In orchestras, the tambourine player rehearses exactly one slap for weeks — make it count.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Tambourine lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Trombone Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A trombone — the brass instrument with a slide instead of buttons. Push the long U-tube out and the note sinks; pull it home and it climbs. It is the only instrument that visibly stretches a sound.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A trombone is brass tubing bent into a loop with a sliding U-section. No valves: the player’s arm chooses the note by lengthening or shortening the tube, and lips buzz the rest.

      What does it sound like?

      Big, bold, gliding brass. Trombones roar in orchestras, strut in jazz bands and own every cartoon slide-whistle moment ever animated — the wah-wah-wah is their signature.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      The slide makes pitch physical and visible: arm out = low, arm in = high. Children who play air-trombone with a full stretch are rehearsing the whole high-low map with their bodies.

      Say it together

      “Wahhh-wOOO-wahhh! The trombone slides like a cartoon voice — down for sleepy, up for surprised.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      One arm is the slide: push it out while your voice sinks — wahhhh — pull it in while your voice climbs — woo! Play three slides: giant yawn down, rocket up, and a slow wobble in the middle.

      Quick parent note

      Trombone players find notes by ear and by arm — there are no marks on the slide. Your stretching arm game is the real skill in disguise, and it scales beautifully to playground size.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Trombone lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Trumpet Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A trumpet — the smallest, boldest brass horn, with three valves and a voice that cuts through a whole orchestra. When the trumpet plays fanfare, everyone in the kingdom knows dinner is served.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A trumpet is a brass tube with a cup mouthpiece and three valves. Buzzing lips make the sound; valves reroute the air to lengthen the tube and drop the pitch — three fingers, many notes.

      What does it sound like?

      Clear, ringing, glorious loudness. Trumpets announce kings, lead parades, sparkle over jazz bands and play the loudest birthday announcements in musical history.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      The trumpet’s lip-buzz secret is a revelation: the instrument only amplifies a raspberry. Children discover that sound comes from THEIR lips — the horn just makes it bigger.

      Say it together

      “Ta-da-ta-DAAA! Bright and royal — the trumpet is the fanfare machine of the Music Room.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Buzz a raspberry into your fist, then pull the fist away slowly — the buzz thins into a trumpet-ish brrrap. Now add three royal notes: ta-ta-ta-DAAA, and bow. Applause is mandatory.

      Quick parent note

      Trumpet mutes are the funny cones that make it go wah — a mute is just a plug that changes the buzz. A paper tube in front of your buzzing fist gives the honest home version.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Trumpet lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Tuba Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A tuba — the enormous coiled grandfather at the back of the brass family, wrapped around its player like a snake wearing a bell. Its voice is the deepest in the room and, somehow, the funniest.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What does it sound like?

      A tuba is the biggest brass instrument: a very long tube coiled around the player, with a wide bell on top and four valves for fingers. All that tubing makes the deepest notes there are.

      What does it sound like?

      The foundation. Tubas hum the low line under the whole band — oom under the pah, wobble under the waltz — and take the comedy solos nobody expects from a giant.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      The tuba completes the high-low ladder started by the piccolo: one card for the ceiling, one for the floor. Deep sounds also slow racing bodies — a tuba song is a legal sedative at bedtime.

      Say it together

      “Bwommm… bwom-bwommm! Deep as a basement, warm as soup — the tuba sings the floor of the music.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Sing your lowest possible note with a hand on your throat to feel the buzz — your inner tuba. Now walk in slow motion while humming it: tuba steps. Fast motion is strictly piccolo-only.

      Quick parent note

      A tuba is so long that uncoiling it would stretch across a room. If your child wraps a blanket around themselves and hums low, that is a tuba costume and it is entirely correct.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Tuba lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Ukulele Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A ukulele — a guitar’s small, sunny cousin from Hawaii with four strings and a neck that fits a four-year-old’s hand. One strum and it smiles: the ukulele is the friendliest real instrument to start on.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A ukulele is a small four-stringed guitar-like instrument from Hawaii. Soft nylon strings are kind to small fingers, the body is light, and simple chords sit within one tiny hand span.

      What does it sound like?

      Sunny strumming. Ukuleles accompany singing better than almost anything — one easy chord, one song, one room of people singing along whether they planned to or not.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      The ukulele is a real instrument sized for real small hands — the confidence ladder from box-guitar to proper strings, with a real song at the top on day one.

      Say it together

      “Plinky-plink! Bright and light as a coconut falling on sand — the ukulele only knows happy songs.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Four strings, four fingers: trace a ukulele on paper, tape it to a table and strum the air strings with a thumb sweep. Sing any song while strumming — the uke rule is singing comes first.

      Quick parent note

      “Ukulele” means jumping flea in Hawaiian — for the fingers dancing on the strings. Two chords make a dozen songs; a real soprano uke costs less than most toys and never needs batteries.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Ukulele lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Violin Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A violin — four strings, a bow, and the closest thing to a human voice that wood and hair can build. It rests on the shoulder, whispers like wind and sings like the star of every fairy tale.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A violin has four strings tuned low to high and a bow of horsehair to draw across them. It sits under the chin on the shoulder — the left hand fingers the notes, the right arm does the singing.

      What does it sound like?

      The melody crown. Violins lead orchestras, waltzes, lullabies and every chase scene: fast bows sparkle, slow bows ache, and the smallest pressure change tells a different story.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      The bow is a long, slow motion — perfect training for the long, slow strokes that later write letters. And the violin’s crying-singing range gives feelings a vocabulary without words.

      Say it together

      “Eeeeee-ahh — high and sweet, sometimes a purr, sometimes a cry. The violin sings while you stroke it.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Arm bow, table violin: stroke one arm slowly with the other while singing aaaa — long bow, long note. Short bows for a running mouse song, long bows for a sleepy moon song. Bow changes tell all.

      Quick parent note

      Small violins exist in fractions — a sixteenth-size fits a three-year-old. Until then, the arm-violin is fully legitimate: every great violinist spent time pretending before the shoulder rest.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Violin lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Xylophone Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A xylophone — a rainbow staircase of wooden bars you strike with mallets, low bars big on the left, high bars small on the right. It is the instrument that makes scales feel like a playground slide.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What is this instrument?

      A xylophone is a row of wooden bars in size order, each on its own frame. Striking a bar with a mallet makes the wood sing; the bigger the bar, the deeper the bonk.

      What does it sound like?

      Crisp, woody, dancing notes. Xylophones play the bouncy tunes, the skeleton-dance rattles and every cartoon moment where someone tiptoes down a staircase.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Size-order bars are a scale you can SEE — the clearest high-low map in music. Running mallets up and down builds the left-low, right-high instinct that keyboards later formalise.

      Say it together

      “Bonk-bonk-binki-bonk! Wooden bars talk in colours — big bar low, little bar high, run down the rainbow.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Line up drinking glasses filled with different water amounts and tap them with a spoon — more water, lower bonk. Order your glass band from biggest bonk to tiniest and play the rain song.

      Quick parent note

      The name starts with X, which is why the card is doubly famous — it bails out every alphabet hunt. In orchestras the xylophone part is played exactly as written: strictly, and with enormous joy.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Xylophone lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Beat Flashcard for Preschoolers

      The beat — the steady pulse underneath every song, the one your foot finds without asking permission. On the card it is two hands tapping a drum; in real life it is everywhere your body already keeps time.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      The beat is the steady pulse of music — the tick every other sound arranges itself around. Clap with a song and your hands will land on it; it is the part bodies cannot ignore.

      Where do we hear it?

      It holds the song together. The beat tells walkers how to walk, clappers when to clap and dancers where the floor is. Lose the beat and even the best song falls over.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Finding and keeping a steady beat is one of the biggest early-learning skills music offers — it feeds walking, cutting, bouncing balls and, later, reading with rhythm. The card makes the invisible visible.

      Say it together

      “Tap-tap-tap-tap! The beat is the steady one — not fast, not slow, just always there, like a heart that learned music.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play a steady tap on your knees — tap-tap-tap — and walk around the room exactly on it. Then tap the beat while a song plays: did your taps and the song agree? If yes, you found it.

      Quick parent note

      Steady beat is not the same as fast: a lullaby has one too, just slower. If your child’s taps drift off, join THEIR tempo and march together — keeping the beat together is the whole game.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Beat lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Clap Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A clap — the instrument you were born carrying. Two hands, one sound, zero setup: claps punctuate every song we sing, and on this card they are the star, not the accompaniment.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      A clap is two hands meeting fast enough to make a snap of air. It is the oldest instrument there is, and the only one always packed and ready.

      Where do we hear it?

      Accent and applause. In songs, claps mark the important beats; after songs, they mark joy. A single well-placed clap can hold a whole room’s attention.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Clap patterns are pure listening memory: clap-clap… clap! Copying them builds the attention and echo skills that language runs on — all disguised as a game children already love.

      Say it together

      “CLAP! One clap says hello, two claps say again, and a clap-pattern says: your turn now.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play the clap-echo game: you clap a pattern — clap, clap-clap, clap — and your child claps it back exactly. Then swap leader. Three rounds is a full music lesson; applause after is automatic.

      Quick parent note

      Clapping in time (not just clapping) is the skill. Start by clapping together at the same instant — hand-over-hand guidance helps — then let the echo game stretch the memory.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Clap lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Dance Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Dance — what music does when it gets into your legs. On this card the word means the whole joyful mess: spinning, stomping, wiggling and freezing, the only Music Room activity where the whole body plays.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Dance is moving your body to music — marching, spinning, stomping, tiptoeing, freezing. Every culture dances, and every child starts before anyone teaches them.

      Where do we hear it?

      Dance turns sound into motion. It is how you can SEE the beat, the tempo and the volume — the music becomes visible in knees and elbows.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Moving to music wires balance, timing and listening together — a full-body coordination class wearing a party costume. Freezing when the music stops is also the world’s best self-control drill.

      Say it together

      “Step-step-spin! When the music plays and your feet join in — that is dancing, and nobody does it wrong.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play freeze dance: music on means dance any way you like, music off means statue. Fast song = fast dance, slow song = slow-motion dance. Three songs and everyone is happily exhausted.

      Quick parent note

      Never fix a child’s dancing — there is no wrong version. Offer challenges instead: “can you dance small as a mouse? tall as a tree?” The card asks the question; their legs answer.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Dance lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Harmony Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Harmony — the magic that happens when different notes sound at the same time and, instead of arguing, they agree. It is why one voice sounds nice but a whole family singing together sounds like home.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Harmony means notes sounding together on purpose — a chord under a melody, a second voice beside the first. The notes are different, and that is exactly why they fit.

      Where do we hear it?

      It makes music rich and warm. A melody alone is a line drawing; harmony is the colouring. Every cosy chord in every lullaby is harmony doing its quiet work underneath.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Harmony is difference turning out to be a good thing — a big idea for small people. Two voices not singing the same note, and the song getting BETTER, is teamwork you can hear.

      Say it together

      “One note is you, one note is me — sing both together and… ahhh! That cozy together-sound is harmony.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      You sing one long note — aaaa. Your child sings another long note at the same time. Listen together: do they fit, or argue? Try again until you find the fit — that agreement is harmony.

      Quick parent note

      Harmony needs two, so this card is a family instrument. If the two notes clash and you both giggle, that also taught the lesson — fitting is a discovery, and discoveries need the misses.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Harmony lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Listen Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Listen — the quietest word in the Music Room and the most powerful. Every song starts by listening, every copy-game runs on it, and this card asks for the most precious thing a busy child owns: their ears.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Listening is paying attention with your ears — catching the sounds instead of letting them rush past. Musicians practise it on purpose; small children are already world champions when they choose to be.

      Where do we hear it?

      It is the door to every other music skill: keeping a beat means hearing it, singing means hearing yourself, and every echo game anywhere starts with two open ears.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Deliberate listening grows attention span, sound memory and the noticing muscle that later reads words and spots patterns. And it is free: the world is already playing.

      Say it together

      “Ears open, voices off… What do you hear? Listening is the game where quiet wins.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play the listening minute: everyone closes eyes for sixty quiet seconds and collects sounds — a fridge hum, a bird, a car, your own breath. Count your finds together and crown the rarest one.

      Quick parent note

      Real listening practice is silent modelling: you go still first, and the room follows. If your child hears something you missed, they lead the next listening minute — turnabout is fair.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Listen lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Lyrics Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Lyrics — the words a song sings. The tune is the ride; the lyrics are where it is taking you. This card celebrates the part of music you could write on paper: the story, the question, the silly bit about the bus.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Lyrics are the words of a song — what the singer says note by note. Some songs have many, some have just one happy word, and both count.

      Where do we hear it?

      They carry meaning. Lyrics tell the story in the song, ask the questions, name the wheels on the bus going round — the melody makes you hum it, the lyrics make you know it.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Sung words are a language workout in disguise: rhymes stretch ears for sounds, repetition builds vocabulary, and children routinely learn new words first from songs and only second from books.

      Say it together

      “The song says words! Sing the tune, then say what it SAYS — the lyrics are the song’s talking part.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Sing a favourite song, then ask: what did the song SAY? Let your child tell the story of the lyrics in their own talking voice — then swap: turn a bedtime instruction into song lyrics and sing it.

      Quick parent note

      Misheard lyrics are a family treasure — whatever your child thinks the words are, write it down. Making up new lyrics to a known tune is the next game, and it never ends.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Lyrics lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Melody Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Melody — the tune itself: the line of notes that walks up and down and gets stuck in your head on the way to dinner. It is the part of every song you would hum back, and this card holds the whole idea in one word.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Melody is a line of notes played one after another — up, down, same note again — that your ear follows like a path. It is what you mean when you say “I know that tune!”

      Where do we hear it?

      It is the part people remember. Instruments may argue underneath and drums may drive, but the melody is the face of the song — the bit you recognise from three notes in.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Melody memory is ear training that feels like fun: noticing when a tune goes up, down or repeats is the exact skill notation will later draw on paper. Bath humming is legitimate practice.

      Say it together

      “La-la-la-LA! The melody is the tune — the part you hum in the bath and whistle on the stairs.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Hum a tiny melody of three notes — la-la-LA — and have your child echo it. Then ask: did it go up at the end or down? Draw it in the air with a finger: up, down, or flat? Melody becomes visible.

      Quick parent note

      Everyone hums before they can name notes — melody is democratic. If your child invents a tune with no name, it is still a melody: record it on a phone and name it after them.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Melody lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Music Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Music — the big word itself, with a smiling note under it. This card is the name of the whole room: organised sound, made by people, kept by families, and the only school subject that is also a feeling.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Music is sound arranged on purpose — singing, drumming, plinking, humming — made to be listened to, moved to and remembered. Every culture on earth makes some.

      Where do we hear it?

      It does everything: it carries songs to sleep, marches parades along, celebrates birthdays, sells soap and survives as the oldest human heirloom there is. The word covers all of it.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Naming the big idea gives children a handle for the whole set: instruments play music, words describe music, people make music. One word, one card, the whole room in a pocket.

      Say it together

      “This whole card set IS music — singing, drums, bells, dancing. Say the big word slowly: muuu-sic.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play the music-or-not game: hum a tune (music!), bang a door (just a door!), sing while washing hands (music!). Let your child be the judge and keep score — the arguments are the curriculum.

      Quick parent note

      Nobody agrees on where music starts and sound ends, and that is a feature. Your child’s verdict on the washing-hands song is as valid as any professor’s — more, probably.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Music lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Pitch Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Pitch — how high or low a sound is. The squeak of a mouse and the growl of a bear can play the same song and only pitch tells them apart. This card is the ladder: high notes at the top, low notes at the bottom.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Pitch is the highness or lowness of a sound — fast vibrations sit high, slow ones sit low. Every voice, string and drum skin has its own spot on the ladder.

      Where do we hear it?

      It builds melodies and voices: a song is notes at different pitches in a row. High pitch finds balloons and babies; low pitch finds bears, bass drums and grandads’ “hello”.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Hearing and making high and low is the ground floor of all music-making — and the arm-up-arm-down game for pitch later becomes the arm for reading notes that climb the page.

      Say it together

      “High like a bird — eeee! Low like a bear — mmmm. Pitch is how high or how low the sound sits.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Hold both hands out: high hands = sing eeee (bird), low hands = sing mmmm (bear). Now play the pitch ladder — hand rises, voice rises; hand sinks, voice sinks. Speed up until someone giggles.

      Quick parent note

      Small voices sit high and light — that is correct, not shy. Low-note growls are equally welcome: the ladder needs both ends, and your child’s bear impression is music theory in costume.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Pitch lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Song Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A song — words and tune joined together so the story can be hummed. This card is the room’s end product: instruments played, words chosen, melody found — and then someone sings the whole thing, start to finish.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      A song is music with words — a melody carrying lyrics from beginning to end. It can be long or three seconds long, brand new or older than the country.

      Where do we hear it?

      It is the unit of joy: happy birthdays, washed behinds, bus wheels and sleep-time moons all arrive inside songs. A song makes words easier to remember and time easier to spend.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Songs are memory technology — everything sung sticks: alphabets, days of the week, shoe-tying steps. Singing together also syncs a room faster than any instruction ever has.

      Say it together

      “Words plus tune equals a song! Sing any song you love — a song is music that knows what it wants to say.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Make a two-line song right now about whatever is in front of you — the dog, the rain, the dinner. Sing it twice. Add a chorus of one word. That is a real song and it belongs to its writer.

      Quick parent note

      Family theme songs work absurdly well: a ten-second song about tidying up will outlast any reminder. The card’s job is permission — every family is a song-writing family when asked.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Song lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Tempo Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Tempo — how fast or slow the music goes. Same song, different tempo, completely different animal: a lullaby at bedtime tempo becomes a marching song at parade tempo. The card is the speed dial of the whole room.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Tempo is the speed of music — how quickly the beats arrive. Composers write it in Italian (largo slow, presto fast) but bodies understand it without any words at all.

      Where do we hear it?

      It decides the mood of the feet: slow tempo makes heavy sleepy giants, fast tempo makes scampering mice, and the exact same song can be both on request.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Tempo is self-regulation practice hiding in a game: matching your body to a given speed — slower than you want, faster than you want — is the skill behind transitions, queues and patience.

      Say it together

      “Slow like a snail… fast like a puppy! Tempo is the speed of the beat — and you are the dial.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      March to a hand-clapped beat: slow tempo, snail parade. Now the same march at puppy tempo. Now YOU clap and I march — the clapper is the tempo boss. Swap jobs after three songs.

      Quick parent note

      The classic tempo experiment: play one song at two speeds and ask which felt like running and which like floating. Children answer instantly, and they are always right.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Tempo lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Tune Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A tune — the bit of music your brain keeps after everything else goes quiet. “I’ve got a tune stuck in my head” is the highest compliment ears give, and this card is the keeper of that sticky magic.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      A tune is a melody you remember — the song-shape that stays with you after the music stops. It is melody that made it all the way into memory.

      Where do we hear it?

      Tunes carry recognition: three notes in and you know the birthday song, the ice-cream van, the show’s beginning. Tuney songs teach, sell, celebrate and get passed between generations.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Remembering and humming tunes is real auditory memory training — the same memory that will later hold letter sounds, number bonds and your home address, all wearing a party hat.

      Say it together

      “You know that song in your head right now? THAT is a tune. Hum yours out loud — tunes want out.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play the tune hunt: hum a famous tune — Happy Birthday — and have your child name it. Then swap: they hum, you guess. End by inventing one brand-new family tune and naming it after the day.

      Quick parent note

      Earworms are the proof that brains love tunes — use them for good: a goodbye tune at the door, a clean-up tune, a shoes-on tune. The stickier the better; that is the technology working.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Tune lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Volume Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Volume — how loud or soft the sound is, from a whisper to a playground roar. It is the first music contrast every baby discovers and the one household dial that never stops being useful: inside voice, outside voice, music voice.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Volume is the loudness of a sound — how much air and energy it carries. Musicians call the levels dynamics and mark them with letters, but families just call it inside and outside voice.

      Where do we hear it?

      It makes music dramatic: the quiet bit before the loud bit is the oldest thrill in showbusiness. Volume also does etiquette — lullabies are quiet on purpose, and so are libraries.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Deliberate loud-quiet play gives children the vocabulary AND the control switch for their own sound. A child who can sing pianissimo on request owns a skill nurseries dream about.

      Say it together

      “Whisper-small… and then HUGE! Volume is how loud the sound is — and the dial is yours to turn.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Sing one song at four volumes: whisper, inside voice, outside voice, and — quietly — giant. Walk the dial up and down on request. Freeze at whisper level: the hardest and funniest setting.

      Quick parent note

      Loud is allowed in the Music Room — that is what the room is for. The game is choosing the volume, not avoiding it: a child who can turn their own dial down was never told, only asked.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Volume lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Band Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A band — friends who bring different instruments and agree on the same beat. Drums, guitars, a singer, somebody’s uncle on the triangle: a band is proof that music is a team sport with better snacks.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Who is this?

      A band is a group of musicians playing together, each on their own instrument. Bands can be two friends or fifteen uncles — the deal is the same: different sounds, one song.

      What do they do?

      They divide the music up: drums keep the beat, guitars carry the tune, the singer tells the story. No one plays everything — that is the whole point and the whole magic.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Bands are turn-taking made audible. A child in a kitchen band learns the big social skill of music: play YOUR part, leave room for theirs, and the song works.

      Say it together

      “One-two-three-four! A band is friends playing together — everybody different, everybody on the same beat.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Form a family band right now: pot-lid cymbals, jar maracas, box guitar, spoon mic. Choose a song everyone knows, count one-two-three-four and play it. Rule one: every instrument gets heard.

      Quick parent note

      Name the band before the first rehearsal — names matter. A family band with a name, one song and a corridor venue is a complete music education with a merch opportunity.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Band lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Chorus Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A chorus — many voices singing the same song at the same time. One voice is nice; a whole chorus of voices together is weather. This card is the sound of a room full of people deciding to be one instrument.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Who is this?

      A chorus is a group of singers performing together — a school choir, a carload of relatives, a whole hall at a wedding. The word also names the repeated bit of a song everyone joins.

      What do they do?

      They turn a song into an event. Choruses sing in unison or in harmony parts, and their job is the same either way: make the room feel bigger than it is.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Singing in a group gives the safest possible belonging: your voice disappears into the big sound, so shy singers join first and find confidence second. Group singing is a legal joy amplifier.

      Say it together

      “Everybody now — a chorus is ALL of us singing! Many voices, one song, twice the joy.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Be a two-person chorus: sing any song you both know, together, at the same time. Then add the whole family at dinner — the chorus grows one person per meal until the neighbours join.

      Quick parent note

      Chorus is also the repeaty bit of a pop song — the part everybody already knows. Point it out in a car song: “HERE comes the chorus!” and watch everyone suddenly participate.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Chorus lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Conductor Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A conductor — the person at the front waving a small stick and silently running the entire orchestra. No instrument, enormous job: with one raised eyebrow and a flick of the baton, a hundred players breathe together.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Who is this?

      A conductor leads an orchestra: they set the speed, shape the loud and quiet, and cue each group of players when it is their moment to sing. The baton just makes the right hand clearer.

      What do they do?

      They keep a hundred people on one beat and one feeling — entrances, endings, surprises, all decided silently in real time. The audience sees poetry; the orchestra reads orders.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Conducting is leadership children can physically copy: the conductor never says a word, yet everyone follows. Taking a turn with the wooden spoon teaches influence without shouting.

      Say it together

      “Whoosh-whoosh! The conductor waves the beat — big waves for loud, tiny waves for quiet, and a fist means STOP.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Hand someone a wooden spoon — the baton. They wave slow, the family sings slow; big waves mean loud, fingers-closed means freeze. Everyone conducts one song. Sunset finale required.

      Quick parent note

      Real conductors mostly listen — the waving is the smallest part. Your home version works the same: the best young conductors are the ones watching faces, not waving hardest.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Conductor lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Duet Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A duet — exactly two musicians sharing one song. Not a crowd, not alone: the polite, sparky middle of music-making where you literally cannot do it without the other person. Best friend energy, set to melody.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Who is this?

      A duet is two musicians playing or singing together — piano and voice, two violins, two friends with one song. Duets are built on trading: one leads, the other answers, then both go together.

      What do they do?

      They balance: nobody hides in a duet and nobody dominates for long. The two players agree on speed, trade the melody back and forth and finish at exactly the same moment.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      A duet is cooperation with a scoreboard you can hear: if one races ahead, the song shows it. Two children holding a tempo together are practising patience, listening and compromise at once.

      Say it together

      “Just us two — you start, I join! A duet is two people and one song, taking turns and then together.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play a kitchen duet: one person keeps the beat on knees, the other hums the tune. Swap roles after one verse. Golden rule — the beat-keeper is the boss, and the boss must be steady.

      Quick parent note

      Duets need no talent floor: pot-lid and spoon qualify. The true duet skill is ending together — practise the big finish separately, then combine, and bow as one unit. Two bows, one song.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Duet lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Orchestra Flashcard for Preschoolers

      An orchestra — a hundred musicians in sections: strings in front, woodwinds behind, brass behind them, percussion at the back. On the card, five children in concert dress carry the whole idea: many instruments, one giant song.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Who is this?

      An orchestra is a very large group of musicians playing together, sorted into families — strings, woodwinds, brass, percussion — each family sitting in its own neighbourhood of the stage.

      What do they do?

      They perform the biggest music humans write: symphonies, film scores, fairy-tale soundtracks. Each section waits, listens and joins on cue — a hundred soloists acting as one voice.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      The orchestra is the ultimate many-hands picture: nobody could play a symphony alone, and nobody needs to. Sections sitting together teach children that big things are built by groups.

      Say it together

      “The orchestra is a whole city of instruments! Strings here, drums there — a hundred friends, one enormous song.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Seat your toys in sections — stuffed animals on strings duty, blocks on percussion. Conduct with the wooden spoon, cue each family in turn, and end with the whole toy orchestra at once.

      Quick parent note

      Watch one real orchestra video and play section-spotting: find the violins, find the big drum, find the conductor’s eyebrow. Attendance at a live family concert is the natural sequel.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Orchestra lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Singer Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A singer — the musician whose instrument is themselves. No case, no mallets, no strings: just breath, a melody and the bravery to open their mouth first. Every song starts because somebody chose to sing it out loud.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Who is this?

      A singer is a musician who performs with their voice. Singers carry the tune and the words, tell the story, and hold the room with nothing but breath and nerve.

      What do they do?

      They are the song’s front door: everyone else plays instruments, the singer IS the instrument. Singers learn breath control, memory for words and the courage to go first.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Singing is the most portable music-making there is — always available, free, and it doubles as feelings-language for children who run out of words long before they run out of volume.

      Say it together

      “La-la-LAAA — the singer leads with their voice! Your mouth is the instrument, and it never leaves home.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Everyone picks one line of a known song and sings it solo — one line each, pass the song around the table. Applaud every single voice. That is a recital, and snacks are traditional.

      Quick parent note

      Every child is a singer until someone tells them otherwise — so never. Wrong notes in a kitchen recital receive the same applause as right ones: the courage is the instrument.

      FLASHCARD · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Solo Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A solo — one musician, one spotlight, the whole room listening. After the band plays together, the soloist steps forward alone: the tiniest word in music with the biggest heartbeat attached to it.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      A solo is one musician playing alone — or the moment one player steps out of the group to play a passage by themselves. Solo means alone, and alone means brave.

      Where do we hear it?

      The solo carries the spotlight: inventing, showing off gently, or holding one long beautiful note while a hundred players wait. Solos are music’s turn to say “now watch this one”.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Solos practise the exact skill show-and-tell needs: being listened to on purpose. A kitchen-table solo — one instrument, one audience, one bow — is public speaking with training wheels.

      Say it together

      “All eyes on ONE — a solo is you and the song, everybody else listening. Deep breath… and go!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Solo time: each person plays or sings something short by themselves while everyone else is audience — then serious applause and one compliment each. The solo slot is sacred; keep it short.

      Quick parent note

      A solo can be three notes long. The rule that matters is the audience’s: complete silence while it happens, applause after. Children who get real audiences at home never fear them.
